Horsfield's bronze-cuckoo Chalcites basalis is a brood parasite that deposits a single egg per host nest [N_R_i = single egg per host nest], a unique reproductive strategy among Australian cuckoos. This obligate parasitism constrains the maximum reproductive rate to approximately 9 attempts per 365 days [F_R_i = approximately 9 attempts per 365 days], though this rate is thermally dependent on the maintenance of a core body temperature near 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C] during active breeding intervals. Under the thermal regime of active metabolism, which averages 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], the species attains sexual maturity at roughly 51 days after hatching [tp = roughly 51 days after hatching], a remarkably rapid pace for a medium-sized brood parasite. This precocious gonadal development is an adaptation to high nest failure rates and limited host availability, ensuring individuals can reproduce early in life. The maximum recorded longevity for the species under field conditions is 15 years [am = 15 years], although most individuals likely survive considerably fewer years due to the stochastic nature of host nest encounters at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. Throughout this lifespan, breeding adults maintain a body temperature that rarely deviates far from 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], even during nocturnal rest periods, reflecting a generally high metabolic rate typical of obligate brood parasites that must remain mobile in search of host nests.

Neonates of Chalcites basalis emerge from the egg at a wet weight of 1.3 grams [Wwb = 1.3 grams], a remarkably small size given the bird's ultimate adult mass. Field observations indicate that newly hatched chicks are completely altricial, lacking any downy feather covering and requiring constant brooding from the host parents to maintain thermogenesis. The incubation period that precedes hatching lasts approximately 12 days [ab = approximately 12 days] when the eggs are maintained at an average temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], a value consistent with typical passerine incubation temperatures. This relatively short embryonic development, though facilitated by the host's attentive incubation, leaves the hatchling with meager endogenous yolk reserves, necessitating rapid acceptance by the host parents if the chick is to survive. The small birth mass likely reflects an evolutionary trade-off between minimizing egg size for stealthy deposition and ensuring the chick has sufficient resources to compete with host offspring for parental provisioning.

As the nestling develops within the host's nest, it undergoes an extraordinary transformation from a 1.3 gram [Wwb = 1.3 gram] neonate to a fully grown fledgling. The ultimate wet weight of a reproductively mature adult Chalcites basalis, measured from field-captured specimens during a long-term banding study, is approximately 20 grams [Wwi = approximately 20 grams], a value that reflects a distinct body plan adapted for agile flight and efficient host nest searching. At this adult mass, the bird achieves a high wing loading relative to other cuckoos of similar size, allowing for rapid, direct flight between host territories. This accelerated growth trajectory requires enormous amounts of protein-rich food from the host parents, with the cuckoo chick often outcompeting any host nestlings present. The species' relatively small ultimate size compared to other members of the Cuculidae likely facilitates exploitation of a wider range of smaller-bodied host species, as the adult can slip into nests that are too small for larger congeners.

The fledgling stage marks the beginning of independent life for the young cuckoo, occurring at 17 days after hatching [tx = 17 days after hatching] under the thermal conditions typical of the species' active period (41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]). At this point, the juvenile has achieved approximately 80 percent of adult body mass and possesses fully developed flight feathers, enabling it to leave the host nest permanently. This rapid fledging interval is unusually short for Cuculidae, though it aligns well with the typical nestling periods of the small passerine hosts that the species exploits. After leaving the nest, the fledgling still relies on host parents for several weeks before attaining full nutritional independence. Following fledging, puberty is reached at 51 days after hatching [tp = 51 days after hatching], enabling the young bird to begin its own reproductive career in the same breeding season if conditions permit at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C].

First reproduction in Chalcites basalis occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], corresponding to the onset of the next breeding season, and this timing is linked to a core temperature regime of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C] during active foraging. This one-year interval between hatching and first breeding is remarkably consistent across the species' range, suggesting a strong endogenous circannual rhythm entrained by photoperiod. The maximum lifespan of 15 years [am = 15 years] in this species is comparable to that of other brood parasitic cuckoos, such as the common cuckoo Cuculus canorus, reflecting a life-history trade-off where high adult survival compensates for the low per-nest success rate typical of obligate parasitism at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. Each year, a female will produce a single egg per host nest [N_R_i = single egg per host nest], and given the frequency of parasitism attempts over a 365-day period, the effective daily reproduction rate remains low.
